name: Violet toothpaste (V34 colour corrector)

lead: Violet toothpaste such as V34 leaves a thin violet tint on the teeth. Because violet sits opposite yellow on the colour wheel, it makes yellowish teeth look whiter right away, for a short time and with no peroxide.

The idea is optical, like colour correction in makeup: the pigment cancels yellow tones visually. It does not remove stain or bleach the tooth. No clinical studies of violet toothpastes were found, so the claims rest on colour theory and user reports.

paras: People use it like a regular toothpaste or leave it on briefly before photos or events. The effect is described as short-lived, so it is used as a quick look, sometimes alongside real whitening.
No safety or efficacy studies were found for this product type. Reported effects are cosmetic and short-lived.

angle.text: Violet toothpaste such as V34 deposits a thin violet layer that offsets yellow tones, so teeth look whiter for a short time. The effect is optical and peroxide-free; no published studies cover it yet.

lead: Violet toothpaste, with V34 as a widely discussed example, is a cosmetic product that deposits a thin violet pigment on the teeth. Proponents say that because violet lies opposite yellow on the colour wheel, it makes yellowish teeth look whiter for a short time, without any peroxide.

Colour theory describes complementary colours as those opposite each other on the colour wheel, and says that mixing complementary lights can yield a neutral grey or white appearance; the same source notes this applies to mixing light and that complementary pigments do not behave identically.[1] This is the principle products of this type are said to rely on.

No clinical studies of violet toothpastes were identified. Dental references describe true whitening as breaking down pigment molecules with peroxide-based agents, which is a different mechanism from a coloured cosmetic layer.[2]

sections.h: How it is said to work
paras: Manufacturers and users describe the violet tint as optically neutralising yellow tones in the visible tooth surface, producing a brighter appearance after brushing or after a short application.[1]
Peroxide bleaching, by contrast, uses hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide to degrade chromogens in or on the tooth.[2]
